content: 1. Administer an initial dose of 100 mg of tigecycline via intravenous infusion, followed by 50 mg IV infusion every 12 hours for a duration of 5 to 14 days. For some cases, the duration may extend to 7 to 14 days. No dose adjustment is necessary for patients with renal impairment, as tigecycline is minimally removed by hemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis. 2. Tigecycline is not indicated for the treatment of diabetic foot infections, as clinical trials failed to demonstrate non-inferiority compared to other treatments. Similarly, it is not approved for hospital-acquired or ventilator-associated pneumonia due to higher mortality rates and reduced efficacy observed in tigecycline-treated patients during comparative clinical trials. 3. Tigecycline has orphan drug designation for the treatment of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). It selectively targets leukemia cells and leukemic stem cells by inhibiting mitochondrial protein synthesis. 4. The safety and efficacy of tigecycline in patients under 18 years of age have not been established. 5. Tigecycline decreases the effectiveness of live bacterial vaccines, such as the BCG vaccine, through pharmacodynamic antagonism. Live bacterial vaccines should not be administered until antibiotic therapy is completed. Similarly, coadministration of tigecycline with the cholera vaccine is contraindicated due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Avoid administering the cholera vaccine to patients who have received systemic antibiotics within 14 days prior to vaccination. 6. Tigecycline may reduce the efficacy of oral microbiota therapies containing bacterial spores due to pharmacodynamic antagonism. Complete antibiotic regimens 2 to 4 days before initiating oral microbiota therapy. 7. Tigecycline can alter intestinal flora, potentially reducing the effectiveness of oral forms of hormones such as conjugated estrogens, estradiol, ethinyl estradiol, levonorgestrel, and mestranol. While the risk of contraceptive failure is low, caution and monitoring are advised. 8. Tigecycline may increase the toxicity of dichlorphenamide, as both drugs can cause metabolic acidosis. Therapy should be modified, and patients should be closely monitored. 9. Tigecycline may increase the levels or effects of digoxin by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Caution and monitoring are recommended. 10. Tigecycline may decrease the levels or effects of vitamins such as biotin, pantothenic acid, pyridoxine, and thiamine by altering intestinal flora. These interactions are minor, apply only to oral forms, and have unknown clinical significance. 11. Tigecycline is FDA-approved for the treatment of complicated skin and skin structure infections (cSSSI), complicated intra-abdominal infections (cIAI), and community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (CABP). However, it is not approved for diabetic foot infections or hospital-acquired/ventilator-associated pneumonia due to lower efficacy and increased mortality risk. 12. An increased risk of all-cause mortality has been reported in tigecycline-treated patients compared to those treated with other agents. Deaths were often due to worsening infections, complications, or underlying comorbidities. Tigecycline should be reserved for situations where alternative treatments are unsuitable. 13. Tigecycline is structurally similar to tetracycline-class antibiotics and may cause similar adverse effects, including photosensitivity, pseudotumor cerebri, and anti-anabolic effects (e.g., increased BUN, azotemia, acidosis, hyperphosphatemia). It should be avoided in patients with known hypersensitivity to tetracyclines. 14. Monotherapy with tigecycline should be avoided in patients with cIAI secondary to clinically apparent intestinal perforation. 15. Tigecycline may cause pancreatitis, including fatal cases. If pancreatitis is suspected, discontinue therapy. Patients typically improve after stopping the drug. 16. Tigecycline may cause fetal harm when administered during pregnancy, including permanent discoloration of deciduous teeth and reversible inhibition of bone growth. Advise patients of potential risks to the fetus if used during the second or third trimester. There is no data on the risk of major birth defects or miscarriage. 17. Tigecycline is present in rat milk, and while systemic exposure to nursing pups is minimal, it is likely that the drug will be present in human milk. The developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding should be weighed against the mother’s clinical need for tigecycline and potential adverse effects on the breastfed child. 18. Tigecycline may cause hypofibrinogenemia. Baseline blood coagulation parameters, including fibrinogen levels, should be obtained and monitored regularly during treatment. 19. Increases in total bilirubin, prothrombin time, and transaminases have been reported in patients treated with tigecycline. Use caution in patients with severe hepatic impairment and reduce the dose as necessary. Monitor patients with abnormal liver function tests for worsening hepatic function and evaluate the risk/benefit of continuing therapy. 20. Prescribing tigecycline in the absence of a proven or strongly suspected bacterial infection is unlikely to benefit the patient and increases the risk of developing drug-resistant bacteria.
